paragraphs: R. Yishmael ben Elisha, High Priest.

(a) In Sefer HaPardes attributed to Rashi, it is written that there was a great sage named R. Elisha. He and his wife were very pious, but their children died young. They prayed to the Lord, He answered their voice, and R. Yishmael was born to them. It elaborates there at length. Kanah, Neḥunya's father, wrote about this R. Yishmael in his book of Kabbalah, reporting in his name: 'I, Yishmael the High Priest, was thirteen years old when I went to Neḥunya ben HaKanah to learn Torah. I asked him to tell me who the Prince of Torah was and what his name was. He answered: His name is Yofiel. Immediately I undertook a fast and separated myself from every pleasure for forty days. Finally I uttered a great Name and brought him down. He descended like a flame of fire, his face like lightning. When I saw him I was terrified; all my limbs came apart, and I recoiled. He said to me: Mortal, what are you doing, that you have disturbed the heavenly retinue? I strengthened myself and said: It is manifest and known before Him who spoke and the world came into being that I did not bring you down for my own honor, but to do my Creator's will. Immediately he said: Mortal, putrid drop, maggot and worm! Although your soul is pure, since it has association with the stricken body, you are impure. Therefore, if you wish me to reveal myself to you, fast for forty days, immerse twenty-four times each day, taste nothing foul, nor any kind of legumes or greens, do not look at a woman, and sit in a dark house. I will instruct you as you desire.' He did so and learned much Torah, as appears in the Gemara, Zohar, and Bahir. He would ascend and descend at will and speak with angels. (שה״ק, folio 29a [title unresolved].) In the first chapter of Berakhot (7), R. Yishmael ben Elisha said: 'Once I entered the innermost sanctuary to burn incense, and I saw Akatriel Yah, the Lord of Hosts, seated upon a high and exalted throne. He said to me: Yishmael, My son, bless Me. I said before Him: Master of the universe, may it be Your will that Your mercy overcome Your anger,' etc. Yuḥasin writes in Seder HaDorot: he despised gain, for a man brought him the first shearing and he would not judge his case, Ketubbot, chapter HaNose (it should read chapter Shenei Dayyanei Gezerot, 105b), and Tanḥuma, parashat Shoftim. 'One who sees him in a dream should expect wisdom.' It is true that Avot deRabbi Natan, end of chapter 40, says: one who sees R. Yishmael in a dream should expect wisdom. The newly printed commentary there writes: because he was High Priest and engaged in the order Kodashim, which is called wisdom in chapter Bammeh Madlikin (31a). But it appears that both erred, for this was said about R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague. It says there: one who sees R. Akiva in a dream should fear calamity (that is, because he was killed); thus one who sees R. Yishmael, his colleague, should expect wisdom. Chapter HaRo'eh (57, beginning of side b) explicitly says: one who sees R. Yishmael ben Elisha in a dream should fear calamity.

(b) Emek HaMelekh, folio 39d, writes that the chapters of Heikhalot of R. Yishmael the High Priest relate: 'That day was Thursday. When grievous tidings came from the great city of Gafim, they seized ten mighty men of Israel, headed by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, R. Yishmael ben Elisha, R. Elazar ben Dama, and R. Yehudah ben Bava, and two thousand Torah scholars from Jerusalem as their ransom [the clause's exact construction requires review]. When R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah saw the decree, he arose and brought me down to the Chariot. I asked Suriel, Prince of the Presence, whether it was a decree from the King of kings. He said: The heavenly court wrote down ten and handed [them] to Samael, etc.; Samael accepted upon himself to bear all the decrees, עשב״ג [unresolved source abbreviation].' R. Yishmael ben Elisha said: 'When I came and reported what the Prince of the Presence had told me, they accepted Heaven's judgment. All the companions rejoiced, and they made that day a feast and celebration before R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah. They said: Let the Nasi begin our rejoicing, and we shall follow. They inclined before us all kinds of music, and we drank wine.' See there at length (40a). It appears there that R. Yishmael ben Elisha was killed after R. Ḥanina ben Teradyon. See Yalkut Reuveni (66d, 67c), and see R. Akiva. In chapter 8 of Semaḥot: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and R. Yishmael ben Elisha were arrested, and the news reached R. Akiva and R. Yehudah ben Bava. In Avot deRabbi Natan, chapter 38: when they seized Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and R. Yishmael ben Elisha, a High Priest son of a High Priest, the lot fell on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; afterward they cut off R. Yishmael ben Elisha's head. In the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (11b): R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest's scalp. He was among those killed by the government. Because of his beauty, the emperor's daughter conceived the desire to strip the skin from his face. She embalmed it in balsam so that it would last without alteration, and it still lies in Rome's treasuries, as Rashi explains; so too Rashi in chapter HaRo'eh. In chapter HaOr VeHaRotev (123a), R. Yishmael ben Elisha's scalp is placed on kings' heads; Rashi explains that this is for sorcery in war.

(c) Yuḥasin writes [in Seder HaDorot, under R. Yishmael and R. Yehoshua ben Korḥa]: 'Rabbenu Ḥananel wrote that R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah ransomed R. Yishmael when he was a child' (meaning R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague). 'This does not seem correct, for R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah ransomed Yishmael ben Elisha.' End of quotation. He writes likewise in Seder HaDorot under R. Yishmael ben Elisha, and here in the order of tannaim under R. Yishmael ben Elisha, meaning the High Priest who was killed; this is explicit. Now Menaḥot (64b) relates that when the Hasmonean kings Hyrcanus and Aristobulus besieged one another, etc. (see Part One), they then said: cursed is the man who teaches his son Greek wisdom, etc. Tosafot writes: at the end of chapter Shetei HaLeḥem (99b), Dama (it should read ben Dama), R. Yishmael's sister's son, asked R. Yishmael: 'Since I have learned the whole Torah, may I learn Greek wisdom?' He applied to him the verse, 'You shall meditate upon it day and night,' etc. This implies that, were it not for 'You shall meditate upon it day and night,' it would be permitted. According to the view that even one who has read only Shema has fulfilled 'It shall not depart,' it implies permission. This concerns a case of need, for perhaps he was close to the government, as they permitted Rabban Gamliel's house. R. Yishmael may have refused him because the public need was not as great as that of Rabban Gamliel's house. Rabbenu Shemuel answered that this was before the decree (meaning that before the decree forbidding Greek wisdom he would have permitted it, but 'You shall meditate upon it day and night' forbade it to him). Tosafot writes that one cannot say so—that ben Dama's question to R. Yishmael preceded the decree—for R. Yishmael lived after the destruction: R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah ransomed him as a child, chapter HaNizzakin (58a). (R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah went to Rome. They told him: there is a child in prison, beautiful-eyed, handsome, with his locks arranged in curls. He went and stood at the prison entrance and said, 'Who gave Jacob for spoil?' etc. The child answered, 'Was it not the Lord, against whom we sinned?' etc. He said: 'I am certain that he will issue rulings in Israel. By the Temple service, I shall not leave here until I ransom him for whatever sum they demand,' etc. Who was that child? R. Yishmael ben Elisha, etc. In Jerusalem Talmud, Horayot, chapter 3, halakhah 7, it mentions R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah ransoming a child, but does not mention that he ransomed R. Yishmael ben Elisha.) There was a case of R. Yishmael ben Elisha's son and daughter being captured by two masters, who said: let us mate them and divide the offspring. They cried all night: he said, 'I, a priest, son of a High Priest, should marry a slave woman?' She said, 'I, a priest's daughter, daughter of a High Priest, should marry a slave?' (See above, R. Tzadok: these were R. Tzadok's son and daughter.) Even the other R. Yishmael, one of the ten martyrs (meaning R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest), did not live so early, for Rabban Gamliel (it should read Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) was killed with him. We say that Hillel, (Shimon), Gamliel, and Shimon exercised their patriarchate during the Temple's last hundred years, and Hasmonean rule ended 103 years before the destruction, etc. Tosafot's statement, 'Even the other R. Yishmael, one of the ten martyrs, did not live so early,' means: perhaps ben Dama, R. Yishmael's sister's son, was the sister's son of the martyred R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, and asked him about Greek learning before the decree. Therefore they wrote that this is impossible: the decree was 103 years before the destruction. Certainly R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest was not [already active] 103 years before the destruction, for he was killed at the destruction or afterward. Presumably, when ben Dama asked him before the decree, R. Yishmael ben Elisha was an adult: his sister's son, who had learned the entire Torah before asking, was presumably an adult, and plainly the R. Yishmael he asked was an adult, at least forty. He would thus have been extremely old when killed. Moreover, at thirteen he went to learn from R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah, who presumably was an adult of forty when teaching him the Torah's secrets. Neḥunya brought him down to the Chariot at the killing of the ten martyrs; thus Neḥunya would have been nearly 170 or more at the destruction, and R. Yishmael ben Elisha over 103 when killed. Examine and you will find it. Rather, ben Dama's question certainly came after the destruction; how can one explain, as Rabbenu Shemuel does, that it preceded the decree? You might object: ben Dama was the sister's son of R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, who was ransomed by R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah in HaNizzakin; but that passage explicitly calls the ransomed child R. Yishmael ben Elisha, as above. This is no difficulty, for I shall write below that the undesignated R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, is R. Yishmael ben Elisha. There were two: R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, and the undesignated R. Yishmael ben Elisha, who was not High Priest; the martyr was his grandfather. Yet the immediately following story of R. Yishmael ben Elisha's son and daughter, who said, 'I am the son of a High Priest,' and 'the daughter of a High Priest,' would mean that the R. Yishmael ben Elisha ransomed by R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah was himself the High Priest. It follows that the R. Yishmael whom R. Yehoshua ransomed after the destruction was the undesignated R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, rather than the martyred R. Yishmael ben Elisha, in accordance with Rabbenu Ḥananel and against Yuḥasin. Yuḥasin's words, that R. Yehoshua ben Ḥananyah ransomed R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, might have seemed somewhat plausible from 'a child beautiful-eyed and handsome,' etc.; Rashi was already cited above that they stripped his facial skin because of his beauty. Tosafot's statement above that the one ransomed by R. Yehoshua was another person, rather than R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, means R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's disputant. This follows Tosafot's identification of R. Akiva's disputant as R. Yishmael ben Elisha and its statement that there were two R. Yishmael ben Elishas, as I shall quote under R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's disputant. But this is as bitter as a lupine: R. Yehoshua ransomed him after the destruction as a child, whereas it is known that R. Elazar ben Azaryah was appointed Nasi about five years after the destruction; see there at length. Mishnah Yadayim, chapter 4, mishnah 3, relates that on that very day of his appointment R. Yishmael said to him, 'Elazar ben Azaryah, you bear the burden of proof, since you rule stringently,' etc.; R. Elazar ben Azaryah answered, 'Yishmael, my brother,' etc. Thus R. Yishmael ben Elisha, R. Akiva's colleague, was an adult at that appointment. How can one say that R. Yehoshua ransomed him after the destruction as a child?

Rather, one must say there were three R. Yishmael ben Elishas: the martyred High Priest; R. Akiva's colleague; and the one who was a child after the destruction, ransomed by R. Yehoshua, who was the martyr's grandson. If so, R. Akiva's disputant, whose father was named Elisha, cannot have been the son of the martyred High Priest. R. Akiva's disputant was an adult five years after the destruction and was born many years before it, when the High Priest was still alive. How could Elisha, the High Priest Yishmael's son, name his own son Yishmael after his father while he was still alive? Nor can one say that R. Akiva's colleague was the martyred High Priest and that the child ransomed by R. Yehoshua was his grandson. It might have seemed somewhat plausible: Shevuot (26a) says that R. Yishmael attended Neḥunya ben HaKanah, who expounded generalizations and particulars, and he likewise expounded generalizations and particulars; R. Akiva attended Naḥum of Gam Zu and expounded, etc. I already quoted above, 'I, Yishmael the High Priest, was thirteen when I went to learn Torah from R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah.' It is difficult that the High Priest and his grandson R. Yishmael ben Elisha, R. Akiva's colleague, should have attended one teacher. Thus the High Priest and R. Akiva's colleague would have to be one. Yet this difficulty proves nothing, for Neḥunya ben HaKanah lived a long life, as R. Akiva asked him, 'By what merit have you lived so long?' (But) [Also] from the following consideration the martyr cannot be R. Akiva's colleague: Dorot Olam, Semaḥot, and the aforementioned Avot deRabbi Natan say that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and R. Yishmael ben Elisha were killed together. It is known that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the Elder was killed on the day of the destruction; they also wished to kill his son, Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, but Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai saved him (see his entry). I already showed above that Mishnah Yadayim explicitly has R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, alive when R. Elazar ben Azaryah was appointed, five years after the destruction. Thus he cannot be the martyred High Priest—unless we say, with Yuḥasin [in Seder HaDorot, under R. Yishmael ben Elisha], that the High Priest was killed after the destruction, against Dorot Olam. The Talmud does suggest he lived afterward: Bava Batra (60b), 'It is taught: R. Yishmael ben Elisha said: From the day the Temple was destroyed, it would be proper to decree upon ourselves not to eat meat,' etc. In the first chapter of Shabbat (12b): 'The rabbis taught: Yishmael ben Elisha said: I shall read and will not tilt [the lamp]. Once he read and tilted it, and wrote in his notebook: When the Temple is rebuilt I shall bring a fat sin-offering,' etc. It says there that R. Yishmael ben Elisha is different because he treats himself as an ordinary person regarding Torah matters. Thus he was killed after the destruction, perhaps long afterward, like R. Akiva, one of the ten martyrs, who was killed fifty-two or seventy-three years after the destruction (see his entry). It could then be that R. Akiva's colleague was the martyred High Priest, still alive at R. Elazar ben Azaryah's appointment five years afterward. Yet we must say, with Tosafot, that there were two R. Yishmael ben Elishas, the martyr and his grandson. R. Yehoshua ransomed the child after the destruction; necessarily he was the grandson of the martyr, who had been High Priest during the Temple's existence and ascended to heaven to learn whether the decree had been issued there, etc. Accordingly, Yuḥasin's proof that R. Yishmael ben Elisha was killed after the destruction—from 'From the day the Temple was destroyed, it would be proper to decree upon ourselves,' and 'When the Temple is rebuilt I shall bring a sin-offering'—proves nothing. Perhaps the speaker was the martyr's grandson, while the martyred High Priest was killed with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel at the destruction, as Dorot Olam, Semaḥot, and Avot deRabbi Natan hold. These matters still require examination and reconciliation, for they are difficult to fit together. But Yuḥasin's statement that the child R. Yishmael ben Elisha whom R. Yehoshua ransomed after the destruction was the martyred High Priest—heaven forbid that one say so! If he is called High Priest, he served while the Temple existed, as above, and entered the innermost sanctuary to burn incense. How could he be a child after the Temple's destruction? (See above, what I wrote in the name of חס״ל [provisionally Ḥesed LeAvraham].) Nor can the child be R. Yishmael ben Elisha, R. Akiva's colleague, since I proved above that he was an adult five years after the destruction. Rather, necessarily the one ransomed by R. Yehoshua was the High Priest's grandson.

In Tosafot, Yevamot (104a): 'R. Yishmael son of R. Yose said: I saw R. Yishmael ben Elisha.' This is difficult: R. Yishmael ben Elisha was killed before R. Akiva, while R. Yishmael son of R. Yose was subordinate to Rabbi, and Rabbi was born on the day R. Akiva died. One must say there were two R. Yishmael ben Elishas: the martyr was the grandfather of the one whom R. Yishmael son of R. Yose saw, for he may have lived long after R. Akiva. End of quotation. See Tosafot, Zevaḥim (119, end of side a): R. Yishmael says, 'Both were Shiloh'; R. Shimon ben Yoḥai says, 'Both were Jerusalem.' Rashi writes that Megillah establishes it according to R. Yishmael, but this is imprecise: in Megillah (10a) it is R. Yishmael son of R. Yose, who lived in Rabbi's days, whereas here it is R. Yishmael ben Elisha, the disputant of R. Akiva, R. Shimon ben Yoḥai's teacher. End of quotation. Tosafot, Zevaḥim (61a), likewise writes that R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague, is R. Yishmael ben Elisha. To remove the confusion, there must therefore have been three: the one killed at the destruction; R. Akiva's colleague, an adult when R. Elazar ben Azaryah became Nasi; and the one whom R. Yishmael son of R. Yose saw. I found a pearl in Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, §15: 'Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai lived at the destruction, and afterward established a study house in Yavneh for forty years. After him the patriarchate returned to Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh' (see his entry). Thus R. Elazar ben Azaryah was appointed after two or three years of Rabban Gamliel, forty-three years after the destruction. Accordingly, the R. Yishmael ben Elisha ransomed by R. Yehoshua as a child after the destruction could have been the martyr's grandson, R. Akiva's colleague, and an adult at R. Elazar ben Azaryah's appointment. Yet these words of Sefer Keritot contradict Rashi at the end of Rosh HaShanah (31, end of side b): Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai exercised the patriarchate after the destruction for only one or two years, followed immediately by Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh. Tosafot writes likewise (see R. Elazar ben Azaryah). On Sefer Keritot's view, what R. Elazar ben Azaryah tithed each year must have been a tax to the king. Examine there: animal tithing ceased after the destruction, and he was eighteen when appointed Nasi, forty-three years afterward. I shall further show you Megalleh Amukot, probably ofan 73 [א׳ ע״ג; edition uncollated]: R. Yishmael was Joseph's reincarnation and R. Akiva Simeon's. This is the secret of R. Akiva's saying to R. Yishmael, 'My brother, I interpret bat and u-vat' [בת ובת, wordplay left visible]; see R. Akiva, what I wrote there. Ḥesed LeAvraham writes that the martyred High Priest was Joseph's reincarnation; see below at length. It would thus appear that R. Akiva's colleague was the martyred High Priest. Return again and again to reconcile all these difficulties. Ḥesed LeAvraham, spring 5, river 25, writes: 'Joseph the righteous one's soul was reincarnated in the martyred R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest. Therefore he was handsome like Joseph and deserving of punishment to repair the flaw of ten sparks of Joseph's drop of semen. Thus they stripped the skin of his face, corresponding to "They stripped his tunic." As Joseph was captive among Egyptians, so R. Yishmael ben Elisha was among gentiles.' End of quotation. This suggests that he holds that the person ransomed by R. Yehoshua was the martyr. I already wrote above of the difficulty with this. See רקנ״ט [provisionally Recanati]: for the sin of 'They stripped Joseph,' R. Yishmael's skin was stripped; see there, Vayeḥi, at 'Jacob said to his sons: Gather.' Gilgulei Neshamot writes: 'R. Yishmael the High Priest is in the mystery of Josiah, before whom there was no king [like him]. In Yalkut Melakhim, §21: a year before his birth he was named, and he rejected idols, etc. So too Metatron was R. Yishmael the High Priest's godfather and foretold his birth to his mother, appearing to her when she went and returned from ritual immersion several times that night. His flesh was stripped just as all Josiah's flesh was made like a sieve. His son and daughter died weeping, as in Gittin, HaNizzakin, above. This repaired Amnon and Tamar, for she was beautiful, and Amnon too handsome and fair. Although they occurred on another occasion in R. Yose of Yukrat's son and daughter (see his entry), she too, Tamar, was not deserving of being the cause. "To punish the righteous is also not good." Just as punishment is exacted from the effect, so it is exacted from the cause.' End of quotation. His colleague: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai (see Shemuel HaKatan). גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael] writes: at Shizur R. Shimon Shezuri is buried; near him is the grave of R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest, one of the ten martyrs, and beside him the grave of R. Shimon ben Elazar.
